disorders.name: Intellectual Disability (Intellectual Developmental Disorder)
disorders.ep_note: Most common reason for EP referral in Ireland. Severity determined by adaptive functioning NOT IQ alone. Always use two standardised measures. NCSE resource teacher allocation requires EP report.
disorders.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by significant limitations in both intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour, originating during the developmental period. Severity (Mild, Moderate, Severe, Profound) is classified by adaptive functioning across conceptual, social and practical domains — not IQ score alone.
disorders.alert: In Ireland, NCSE allocation for Resource Teaching requires a current EP report. Severity classification must be based on adaptive functioning. Never rely on IQ alone — this is a clinical and ethical requirement under DSM-5-TR.
criteria: Deficits in intellectual functions confirmed by clinical assessment and standardised intelligence testing: reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, academic learning, learning from experience
Deficits in adaptive functioning: failure to meet developmental and sociocultural standards for personal independence and social responsibility in conceptual, social and practical domains
Onset during the developmental period
cognitive_mechanisms: Slower processing speed
Working memory limitations
Reduced rate of learning — longer to acquire and consolidate skills
Weak generalisation across contexts
Difficulties with abstract and symbolic reasoning
differential: Specific Learning Disorder (average IQ + specific skills deficit)
Language Disorder (verbal IQ suppressed — use non-verbal measures)
Environmental deprivation (always consider EAL, neglect, limited opportunity)
Hearing or visual impairment (rule out before testing)
risk_factors: Genetic syndromes (Down syndrome, Fragile X, Prader-Willi)

assessment_tools.name: WISC-V
assessment_tools.purpose: Full Scale IQ and five index scores. Use Nonverbal Index if language barriers present.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Primary cognitive measure for EP reports in Ireland/UK — most accepted by NCSE and NEPS.

assessment_tools.name: DAS-II
assessment_tools.purpose: Differential Ability Scales — particularly useful for younger children and lower ability ranges.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Good floor for low-range assessments; cleaner basal-ceiling structure.

assessment_tools.name: Leiter-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Fully non-verbal measure — for children with language impairments, EAL, or motor difficulties.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Use when verbal mediation would confound results.

assessment_tools.name: Vineland-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Gold standard for adaptive functioning — Communication, Daily Living, Socialisation, Motor domains. Parent/caregiver interview form.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Mandatory companion to cognitive testing for ID diagnosis. Also informs IEP targets.

assessment_tools.name: ABAS-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Adaptive Behavior Assessment System — home and school forms for cross-setting comparison.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful when school and home adaptive profiles differ significantly.

Learning & Attainment: Extremely slow acquisition of new concepts despite repeated teaching
Significant below-grade attainment across all curriculum areas
Difficulty with abstract, symbolic and representational tasks
Limited generalisation of learning to new contexts or settings
Behaviour & Independence: Heavy reliance on adult guidance — difficulty working independently
Needs significant scaffolding for tasks peers manage independently
May appear compliant but not truly understanding

home_signs: Delayed independence in self-care (dressing, hygiene, meals)
Difficulty managing daily routines without adult support
Limited money, time and safety awareness
Needs support with tasks age-peers do independently
ep_formulation: Referral concern: attainment significantly below peers, slow learning rate
Cognitive assessment: WISC-V or DAS-II — establish FSIQ and index profile
Adaptive functioning: Vineland-3 parent interview + teacher ABAS
Developmental and medical history: pregnancy, milestones, previous assessments
Consider: EAL, attendance, vision/hearing, socioeconomic factors
Formulate: profile of strengths and needs across domains
Recommend: IEP with functional targets; SNA allocation; NCSE resource teaching

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Explicit instruction with task analysis, mastery learning and errorless teaching — sequenced, cumulative curriculum

interventions.label: Behavioural
interventions.text: Positive Behavioural Support (PBS) — function-based behaviour support plans where needed

interventions.label: School / NCSE
interventions.text: IEP with SMART targets across conceptual, social and practical domains; NCSE resource teacher and/or SNA allocation via SET hours

interventions.label: Family
interventions.text: Parent partnership in daily living skills; home-school consistency; connecting families with NCSE/Inclusion Support services

classroom_strategies: Simplified, concrete step-by-step instructions
Visual schedules, task boards and first-then prompts
Task breakdown — one small step at a time
Over-learning through varied repetition
Extended time and reduced volume of work
Peer pairing with supportive classmates
Celebratory approach to small incremental progress
parent_strategies: Structured daily routines with visual supports at home
Teach daily living skills in natural contexts (e.g. cooking, shopping)
Connect with NCSE local special education organisers
Use same language and visual supports as school
research_links: NCSE Policy Advice Paper No. 4 — Supporting Students with ID (2011)
EPSEN Act 2004 — Ireland (Educational context)
American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD) guidelines
Emerson & Hatton — Health inequalities and ID
Vineland-3 — Sparrow, Cicchetti & Saulnier (2016)

disorders.name: Global Developmental Delay
disorders.ep_note: Provisional diagnosis for under-5s where standardised assessment is not yet valid. Always reassess after age 5. EP role is often consultation to early years settings and families.
disorders.definition: Significant delay in two or more developmental domains — motor, language, cognitive, social and adaptive — in children under 5 years of age, where severity level cannot yet be reliably assessed by standardised instruments.
disorders.alert: GDD is a provisional diagnosis. Must be reassessed fully after age 5 when standardised cognitive testing becomes reliable. EP should coordinate early years MDT referrals, not diagnose.
criteria: Significant delay in two or more developmental domains
Age under 5 years at time of assessment
Severity cannot be reliably assessed by standardised instruments
cognitive_mechanisms: Immature neural development across multiple systems
Delayed language acquisition impacting all learning
Reduced processing speed
Motor planning difficulties

assessment_tools.name: Griffiths-III
assessment_tools.purpose: Comprehensive developmental scales birth–6 years across 5 domains.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Gold standard for under-5 developmental profiling in Ireland/UK.

assessment_tools.name: Bayley-4
assessment_tools.purpose: Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development — cognitive, language, motor.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Used by MDT; EP may review or contribute to Bayley-based profiles.

assessment_tools.name: ASQ-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Ages and Stages Questionnaire — parent-completed developmental screening.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful for early years consultation — can advise staff on use.

assessment_tools.name: Vineland-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Adaptive behaviour across domains — usable from birth.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Provides baseline adaptive profile useful for early intervention planning.

Early Years Setting: Delayed play skills — parallel play when peers engage cooperatively
Slow motor skill development (fine and gross)
Communication: Does not point or gesture where expected
Limited response to name or instruction

home_signs: Later reaching developmental milestones than peers
Difficulty with self-care compared to same-age children
Limited variety in play
Family expressing concern about development
ep_formulation: Consultation to early years setting — not individual assessment unless indicated
Review MDT developmental reports (paediatrics, SLT, OT)
Advise on early years support and transition planning
Support school on reasonable adjustments
Plan reassessment timeline after age 5

interventions.label: Early Intervention
interventions.text: Intensive multi-domain early intervention (Portage, HSE Early Intervention teams) — most effective under age 5

interventions.label: Early Years
interventions.text: AIM (Access and Inclusion Model) in Ireland — universal and targeted supports for pre-school inclusion

interventions.label: Family
interventions.text: Portage home visiting; parent implementation of early language and play activities; Hanen 'It Takes Two to Talk'

classroom_strategies: Highly structured, predictable environment
Key worker relationship
Visual and gestural prompts
Sensory-supportive room
Simplified language and reduced verbal load
parent_strategies: Portage home visiting where available
Early referral to HSE Early Intervention Team
AIM support for pre-school — access via NCSE
Consistent multi-agency communication
research_links: AIM Policy Framework — NCSE (2016)
HSE Early Intervention Services
Portage Ireland
NCSE — Early Childhood Inclusion guidance

disorders.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
disorders.ep_note: Major EP role in Ireland/UK: contributing to multi-disciplinary diagnostic assessments, post-diagnostic educational planning, and school consultation. ADOS-2 and ADI-R are gold standard — EP may administer ADOS-2.
disorders.definition: A neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests and activities, present from early development and causing functional impact across settings.
disorders.alert: Females are significantly underdiagnosed — they mask and internalise differently. Always assess sensory processing, executive function, and anxiety as part of EP profile. Post-school diagnosis (PDA profile) increasingly common in adolescents.
criteria: A1: Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity (reduced back-and-forth conversation, difficulty sharing interests or emotions, reduced initiation of social interaction)
A2: Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviours (poor integration of verbal and nonverbal communication, limited eye contact, body language or gesture)
A3: Deficits in developing and maintaining relationships (difficulty adjusting behaviour across contexts, difficulty making friends, lack of interest in peers)
B1: Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech
B2: Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, ritualised patterns, distress at small changes
B3: Highly restricted, fixated interests of abnormal intensity or focus
B4: Hyperreactivity or hyporeactivity to sensory input, or unusual interest in sensory aspects of environment
Symptoms present from early developmental period (may not fully manifest until social demands exceed capacity)
Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
cognitive_mechanisms: Executive function differences: planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibition, working memory
Weak central coherence: strong detail-focused processing, difficulty seeing 'the big picture'
Theory of mind differences: difficulty inferring others' mental states
Monotropism: narrow, deep attentional focus on interests
Interoception differences: difficulty reading internal body signals
Enhanced systemising: strong drive to understand and build systems
differential: Social Communication Disorder (SCD): no restricted/repetitive behaviours present
ADHD: social difficulties secondary to inattention/impulsivity — no ASD features
Intellectual Disability: may co-occur — assess both independently
Social Anxiety Disorder: fear of social situations vs social communication difference
Language Disorder: communication difficulties without ASD features
OCD: repetitive behaviours with ego-dystonic quality vs ASD rigidity
risk_factors: Preterm birth and low birth weight
Male sex — but females increasingly recognised as underdiagnosed

assessment_tools.name: ADOS-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule — structured observational assessment across all modules (Toddler, 1, 2, 3, 4). Administered by trained clinician.
assessment_tools.ep_note: EPs can train to administer ADOS-2. Essential for formal diagnostic contribution. Use across all language levels.

assessment_tools.name: ADI-R
assessment_tools.purpose: Autism Diagnostic Interview — Revised. Detailed developmental and behavioural history interview with parent/carer.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Often administered by psychologist or psychiatrist in MDT. Covers first 5 years extensively.

assessment_tools.name: DISCO
assessment_tools.purpose: Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders — particularly useful for females, PDA profile, atypical presentations.
assessment_tools.ep_note: More sensitive for females and late-diagnosed adults. Broader than ADI-R.

assessment_tools.name: SCQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Social Communication Questionnaire — 40-item parent questionnaire screening for ASD features.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful for triage decisions and monitoring. Score ≥15 indicates further assessment warranted.

assessment_tools.name: SRS-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Social Responsiveness Scale — dimensional severity measure across social awareness, cognition, communication, motivation, restricted behaviours.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Good for capturing severity in school and home contexts. Sensitive to school-based needs.

assessment_tools.name: WISC-V
assessment_tools.purpose: Full cognitive profile — expect scatter. Processing Speed and Working Memory indices often lower.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Uneven profile common in ASD. Visual Spatial often a relative strength. Inform curriculum differentiation.

assessment_tools.name: Vineland-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Adaptive functioning — often shows scatter disproportionate to IQ in ASD (high IQ + low adaptive scores).
assessment_tools.ep_note: Helps quantify real-world functional impact beyond cognitive score.

Social & Communication: Difficulty joining group work or play
Takes language literally — misses humour, sarcasm, idioms
Limited peer interaction at break times
Prefers adult company or solitary activity
Behaviour & Sensory: Distress at transitions, noise, unexpected changes
Rigid adherence to routines and rules
Sensory sensitivities to noise, light, texture, smell
Learning: Strong knowledge in areas of special interest
Difficulty with inference and comprehension in texts
Challenges with open-ended tasks and group projects
Executive function difficulties: planning, starting, organising

home_signs: Rigid routines — significant distress when changed
Intense focused interests consuming much of leisure time
Sensory sensitivities (food textures, clothing tags, noise)
Post-school restraint collapse — meltdowns at home after 'holding it together' at school
Difficulty in novel or unstructured social settings
ep_formulation: Referral: social difficulties, behaviour concerns, or parental/teacher concern about ASD
Gather: developmental history from parents; teacher observations; previous reports
Assess: ADOS-2 (direct observation); cognitive profile (WISC-V); adaptive functioning (Vineland-3)
Contribute to MDT: EP role in diagnostic formulation alongside SLT, psychiatry, paediatrics
Post-diagnosis: educational needs assessment — EHC Plan (UK) / IEP (Ireland); school consultation

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: TEACCH Structured Teaching — visual structure, predictability, work systems and physical organisation

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Social Communication Intervention Programme (SCIP) — manualised school-based social communication support

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy adapted for ASD (CBT-ASD) — anxiety and emotional regulation

interventions.label: School / EP
interventions.text: Whole-school autism awareness training; sensory environment audit; EP consultation model with class teachers and SENCOs/SETs

interventions.label: Family
interventions.text: EarlyBird or EarlyBird Plus (NAS — for parents of newly diagnosed children); Autism-specific parent support groups

classroom_strategies: Visual timetables and advance notice of changes
First-then boards for transitions
Sensory accommodations: ear defenders, designated quiet space, flexible seating
Clear, unambiguous written instructions
Interest-based learning hooks and motivators
Limit figurative language — be explicit
Flexible response formats (written, verbal, drawn)
Named trusted adult for support and self-regulation
parent_strategies: Provide advance notice of changes and transitions
Use special interest as a bridge to learning and communication
Allow post-school decompression time before demands
Consistent routines across home and school
Autism Ireland / NAS / Autism Education Trust resources
research_links: NICE NG142 (2021) — Autism in under 19s: support and management
Autism Education Trust — Frameworks and school resources
NCSE — Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Practical Guide for Teachers (2011)
Lai et al. (2020) — Camouflaging of autistic traits in women
SPELL framework — NAS (Structure, Positive, Empathy, Low arousal, Links)

disorders.name: ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder)
disorders.ep_note: One of the most common EP referral reasons. EP role: psychoeducation, cognitive profiling, school consultation, advising on accommodations, contributing to multi-agency assessment. ADHD significantly underdiagnosed in females.
disorders.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent, impairing patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, inconsistent with developmental level, present in two or more settings, with onset before age 12.
disorders.alert: ADHD is substantially underdiagnosed in females — inattentive presentation without hyperactivity is missed. Always screen for comorbid anxiety, dyslexia, DCD and emotional dysregulation. Medication is not the first step — EP consultation, parent training and school strategies come first.
criteria: Inattention (6+ symptoms, ≤5 for 17+): careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention, seems not to listen, fails to finish tasks, difficulty organising, avoids sustained mental effort, loses things, easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, forgetful in daily activities

Hyperactivity-Impulsivity (6+ symptoms, ≤5 for 17+): fidgets, leaves seat, runs/climbs inappropriately, cannot play quietly, acts as if 'driven by a motor', talks excessively, blurts out answers, difficulty waiting turn, interrupts or intrudes
Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12
Symptoms present in two or more settings (school, home, social, workplace)
Clear evidence of clinically significant interference with functioning
Not better explained by another mental disorder
cognitive_mechanisms: Executive function deficits: inhibition (core deficit), working memory, planning, flexibility, initiation
Delayed discounting of rewards — difficulty valuing future over immediate reward
Emotional dysregulation — heightened and rapid emotional responses
Variable alertness and arousal — not consistently inattentive
Weak time perception — time blindness
differential: Anxiety (can present as inattention — worry consumes attention)
Trauma/PTSD (hypervigilance mimics hyperactivity; dissociation mimics inattention)
ASD (executive function overlap — always screen for both)
Language Disorder (processing difficulties may look like inattention)
Specific Learning Disorder (frustration-based avoidance looks like ADHD)
Sleep disorders (sleep deprivation significantly impairs attention)
risk_factors: Male sex — but females increasingly recognised

assessment_tools.name: Conners-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Parent, teacher and self-report forms — DSM-5 aligned scales for inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity. Multiple informants essential.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Most widely used standardised ADHD rating scale in Ireland and UK EP practice.

assessment_tools.name: SNAP-IV
assessment_tools.purpose: Swanson, Nolan and Pelham ADHD rating scale — free, quick teacher/parent form.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful for monitoring pre/post intervention. Available free online.

assessment_tools.name: BRIEF-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Behaviour Rating Inventory of Executive Function — parent and teacher forms. Measures real-world EF impact.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Essential complement to cognitive testing — often more sensitive to daily EF difficulties than WISC.

assessment_tools.name: WISC-V
assessment_tools.purpose: Working Memory Index and Processing Speed Index often impaired. Full profile needed to identify SLD comorbidity.
assessment_tools.ep_note: PSI and WMI typically lower in ADHD. Aids identification of learning needs alongside ADHD.

assessment_tools.name: SDQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire — hyperactivity scale as initial screen.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Used in NEPS school consultations and nationwide in Ireland for initial concerns.

assessment_tools.name: CPT-3 / QB Test
assessment_tools.purpose: Continuous Performance Test — objective attention and impulsivity measure.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful for supporting diagnosis where subjective ratings are inconsistent or contested.

Learning: Inconsistent quality — good days and poor days
Better performance in novel or highly stimulating tasks
Behaviour & Organisation: Poor time management — last to finish or rushes
Social & Emotional: Impulsive social behaviour — doesn't wait, intrudes
Low self-esteem linked to repeated failure experiences

home_signs: Messy bedroom and disorganised personal space
Forgets tasks mid-completion without prompting
Impulsive behaviour and poor risk assessment
Emotional dysregulation — rapid intense reactions
Difficulty falling asleep (very common in ADHD)
Homework wars — takes significantly longer than peers
ep_formulation: Referral: attainment below potential, behaviour concerns, or parental concern
Multi-informant approach: Conners-3 from parent and teacher; BRIEF-2
Cognitive profile: WISC-V — particularly PSI and WMI; check for SLD
Classroom observation: EP direct observation in school setting
Developmental history: early presentation, family history
Formulate: ADHD subtype + any comorbidities; functional impact in school
Recommend: school accommodations; parent training; CAMHS/paediatric referral for medication if indicated

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Parent Management Training (NICE first-line for under 12s): Incredible Years, Triple P, New Forest Parenting Programme

interventions.label: Behavioural
interventions.text: School-based behaviour support: daily report cards, contingency management, immediate specific praise

interventions.label: Executive Function
interventions.text: Executive function coaching and metacognitive strategy training — particularly for secondary-age pupils

interventions.label: Medical Pathway
interventions.text: Referral to CAMHS or paediatrics for medication assessment (methylphenidate/lisdexamfetamine) where appropriate — after behavioural interventions trialled

interventions.label: School Accommodations
interventions.text: IEP/IEAP with EF-based accommodations; SEN support; NCSE resource teaching allocation

classroom_strategies: Preferential seating — front, near teacher, low distraction zone
Chunk instructions — no more than 2–3 steps at a time
Regular movement breaks (planned, not punitive)
Timer use for task transitions
Check-in/check-out system with trusted adult
Immediate specific praise — catch them being good
Written reminders and checklists
Reduce copying from board
Flexible task completion formats
parent_strategies: External organisation systems: visual calendars, colour-coded timetables, checklists
Homework in short timed bursts with planned breaks
Physical activity before homework
Consistent bedtime routine — address sleep hygiene
Specific praise rather than general praise
research_links: NICE NG87 (2018) — ADHD: diagnosis and management
NCSE Research Report — ADHD and Educational Supports
Barkley (2015) — Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Handbook for Diagnosis and Treatment
Cooper & Bilton — ADHD: Research, Practice and Opinion
ADDISS School Guidance — UK resources

disorders.name: Specific Learning Disorder — Reading (Dyslexia)
disorders.ep_note: Major EP assessment role in Ireland (RACE guidelines) and UK (access arrangements). Dyslexia assessment requires dual discrepancy — reading significantly below expectation given cognitive ability AND adequate instruction provided.
disorders.definition: A specific neurodevelopmental learning disorder affecting reading accuracy, fluency and/or comprehension, underpinned by core difficulties in phonological processing, rapid naming and/or verbal working memory — in the context of otherwise adequate instruction and broadly average cognitive ability.
disorders.alert: Dyslexia persists into adulthood. Always confirm adequate instruction has been provided. In Ireland, the RACE scheme enables reading exemption from Irish — EP report required. UK access arrangements (extra time, reader) also require EP evidence.
criteria: Persistent difficulties in reading despite targeted intervention: word reading accuracy, reading rate or fluency, reading comprehension
Affected reading skills substantially and quantifiably below chronological age
Learning difficulties began during school-age years
Not better explained by intellectual disability, uncorrected visual/hearing impairment, other neurological disorders, or inadequate instruction
cognitive_mechanisms: Phonological awareness deficit — core underlying deficit
Rapid Automatised Naming (RAN) deficit — slow retrieval of letter/word names
Phonological working memory deficit — reduced verbal memory span
Orthographic processing weakness — slow sight word development
Delayed letter-sound correspondence automaticity
differential: Language Disorder: broad language difficulties beyond reading
Inadequate instruction or opportunity — always rule out
risk_factors: EAL learners — more complex assessment needed

assessment_tools.name: YARC
assessment_tools.purpose: York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension — accuracy, fluency and comprehension. Standardised norms.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Most widely used standardised reading battery in UK/Ireland EP practice. Use for diagnostic and progress monitoring.

assessment_tools.name: WIAT-III
assessment_tools.purpose: Wechsler Individual Achievement Test — reading, spelling, written language and maths composites.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Provides discrepancy analysis against cognitive ability using same normative sample as WISC-V.

assessment_tools.name: CTOPP-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Comprehensive Test of Phonological Processing — phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Essential for establishing phonological basis of reading difficulties — required for dyslexia diagnosis.

assessment_tools.name: PHAB-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Phonological Abilities Battery — phonological processing components.
assessment_tools.ep_note: UK standardised alternative to CTOPP; established norms for UK population.

assessment_tools.name: TOWRE-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Test of Word Reading Efficiency — timed real word and nonsense word reading.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Sensitive to reading fluency difficulties; useful for identifying double deficit patterns.

Reading: Slow, laboured reading relative to age
Guesses from initial letter rather than decoding
Avoids reading aloud — embarrassment and distress
Difficulty with unfamiliar or technical vocabulary
Writing & Spelling: Slow written output relative to verbal ability
Difficulty copying from board accurately and quickly

home_signs: Avoids reading for pleasure — strong preference for other media
Homework takes disproportionately longer than peers
Frustration and emotional distress around literacy tasks
Strong verbal ability inconsistent with poor reading
ep_formulation: Referral: reading/spelling significantly below expectations, frustration with literacy
Cognitive assessment: WISC-V — establish ability profile (Verbal Comprehension often strong)
Phonological processing: CTOPP-2 or PHAB-2
Reading assessment: YARC or WIAT-III Reading
Confirm adequate instruction was provided
Formulate: dyslexia diagnosis with evidence of phonological basis + reading impact + cognitive discrepancy
Recommend: Structured Literacy; access arrangements (RACE, exam accommodations); technology supports

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Structured Literacy (Orton-Gillingham based): systematic, cumulative, multisensory phonics — strongest evidence base

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Reading fluency interventions: Repeated Reading, Partner Reading, timed rereading

interventions.label: School / Access
interventions.text: RACE scheme (Ireland) — Reading Exemption from Irish with EP report; UK access arrangements — extra time, reader, computer

interventions.label: Metacognitive
interventions.text: Comprehension strategy instruction; working memory support strategies; metacognitive reading approaches

classroom_strategies: Explicit, systematic phonics instruction (not incidental word-learning)
Text-to-speech technology (Claro, Immersive Reader, Voice Dream)
Extended time for all reading and writing tasks
Do not ask to read aloud without advance preparation
Pre-teach key vocabulary before reading tasks
Reduce board copying — provide printed notes
parent_strategies: Audio books alongside print — maintain reading exposure
Short daily paired reading with supportive adult
Never shame around reading errors — celebrate attempts
Investigate exam access arrangements early (secondary school)
research_links: Rose Report (2009) — Independent review of early reading
Irish Learning Support Association (ILSA) — Dyslexia and schools
British Dyslexia Association — Evidence-based practice guides
Elliott & Grigorenko (2014) — The Dyslexia Debate
CTOPP-2 — Wagner, Torgesen, Rashotte & Pearson (2013)

disorders.name: Specific Learning Disorder — Mathematics (Dyscalculia)
disorders.ep_note: Less frequently assessed than dyslexia but equally impactful. Core number sense deficit distinguishes dyscalculia from maths underachievement. Key for Junior/Leaving Cert accommodations in Ireland.
disorders.definition: A specific neurodevelopmental learning disorder characterised by persistent difficulty with number sense, numerical facts, calculation accuracy and fluency, and/or mathematical reasoning, despite adequate instruction and broadly average cognitive ability.
disorders.alert: Maths anxiety is common secondary to dyscalculia but is distinct — always assess both. Turner syndrome and Fragile X (females) have higher rates. Calculator access and accommodation are appropriate reasonable adjustments.
criteria: Persistent difficulties in maths despite intervention: number sense, memorisation of arithmetic facts, accurate or fluent calculation, accurate mathematical reasoning
Affected skills substantially below age expectations
Onset during school-age years
Not better explained by intellectual disability, sensory impairments, or inadequate instruction
cognitive_mechanisms: Core number sense deficit — approximate number system impairment
Spatial processing weakness — difficulty with visual-spatial aspects of maths
Procedural learning difficulties — cannot automate calculation procedures
Working memory overload during multi-step calculations
differential: ADHD: careless errors from inattention, not number sense deficit
Maths anxiety (secondary to dyscalculia or primary)
Language Disorder: word problem comprehension difficulties
Dyslexia: impacts reading of maths problems
risk_factors: Turner syndrome (all females should be screened)

assessment_tools.name: Butterworth Dyscalculia Screener
assessment_tools.purpose: Numerosity and arithmetic speed — identifies core number sense deficit.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Quick, standardised screening tool. Good starting point for dyscalculia query.

assessment_tools.name: WIAT-III Maths
assessment_tools.purpose: Numerical operations, maths problem solving and maths fluency composites.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Provides discrepancy from cognitive ability. Links to WISC-V for profile analysis.

assessment_tools.name: KeyMath-3 DA
assessment_tools.purpose: Diagnostic assessment of mathematical conceptual understanding — 10 subtests.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Identifies specific areas of maths difficulty to inform targeted intervention.

Mathematics: Cannot recall multiplication tables despite years of practice
Loses track of steps in multi-step calculations
Cannot estimate or check whether answers are reasonable
Difficulty with mental arithmetic even for simple sums
Wider Impact: Poor time sense — frequently late, difficulty managing time

home_signs: Cannot independently manage money or make change
Difficulty telling analogue time
Gets lost on familiar routes
Avoids number-related tasks
ep_formulation: Referral: persistent maths difficulty despite teaching, inconsistent with other abilities
Cognitive: WISC-V — check Visual Spatial Index and Processing Speed
Maths achievement: WIAT-III or KeyMath-3
Number sense screening: Butterworth Dyscalculia Screener
Rule out: ADHD, maths anxiety, language difficulties in word problems
Formulate: dyscalculia profile with core number sense deficit confirmed
Recommend: CPA approach; calculator access; exam accommodations

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract (CPA/Singapore Maths) — systematic representational progression

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Number Sense interventions: Number Rockets (Tier 2/3); Catch Up Numeracy

interventions.label: Reduce WM Load
interventions.text: Calculator access at all times; number lines, multiplication charts, worked examples provided

classroom_strategies: Multiplication table chart available at all times
Calculator access for calculation-heavy tasks
Worked examples displayed during practice
CPA progression for new concepts
Graph paper for column alignment
Extended time for maths assessments
parent_strategies: Number games rather than rote drilling
Real-world maths in natural contexts (shopping, cooking)
Never share own maths anxiety
Contact NCSE/school SENCO regarding exam accommodations
research_links: Butterworth et al. (2011) — Dyscalculia: From Brain to Education
EEF — Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3
National Centre for Excellence in Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM)

disorders.name: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD / Dyspraxia)
disorders.ep_note: Frequently co-occurs with ADHD and dyslexia. EP role: identify motor difficulties impacting school participation, advise on OT referral, recommend classroom accommodations for handwriting and PE.
disorders.definition: Significant motor coordination impairment that interferes with activities of daily living and academic achievement, not explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment or neurological conditions affecting movement.
disorders.alert: DCD is frequently missed — children are often labelled as 'clumsy', 'lazy' or 'messy' rather than identified as having a real motor learning disorder. Handwriting and PE are major impact areas.
criteria: Acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills substantially below expected for chronological age and learning opportunity
Motor skill difficulties significantly interfere with activities of daily life, academic productivity, leisure and play
Onset in early developmental period
Not better explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment, or neurological condition affecting movement
cognitive_mechanisms: Motor planning deficits — ideational and ideomotor
Internal forward modelling weakness — difficulty predicting movement outcomes
Proprioceptive processing differences
Slow motor learning rate — needs more practice than peers
differential: Hemiplegia or neurological motor disorder (refer to paediatrics)

assessment_tools.name: Movement ABC-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Manual dexterity, aiming and catching, balance — standardised across ages 3–16.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Gold standard motor assessment tool. Below 5th percentile indicates likely DCD. EPs should administer or refer to OT.

assessment_tools.name: DCDQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Developmental Coordination Disorder Questionnaire — parent report screening tool.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Quick parent screen; positive result indicates Movement ABC-2 needed.

assessment_tools.name: Beery VMI
assessment_tools.purpose: Visual Motor Integration, Visual Perception and Motor Coordination subtests.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful to identify visual-motor contribution to handwriting difficulties.

Motor: Difficulty using scissors, rulers, art materials
Slow to change for PE — buttons, zips, laces
Bumps into furniture and peers frequently
Learning Impact: Slow written output disproportionate to verbal ability

home_signs: Slow at getting dressed and undressed
Messy eating — spills frequently
Avoids physical play, sports and cycling
Resistant to tasks requiring fine motor precision
ep_formulation: Referral: handwriting difficulties, PE avoidance, motor clumsiness
Screen: DCDQ parent report
Motor assessment: Movement ABC-2 (EP or OT)
Visual-motor: Beery VMI
Check for: ADHD, dyslexia co-occurring
Formulate: DCD profile + functional impact in school and daily life
Recommend: OT referral; handwriting programme; typing tuition; adapted PE

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: CO-OP (Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance) — metacognitive OT-delivered intervention; strongest evidence for DCD

interventions.label: School
interventions.text: Occupational Therapy school consultation; touch-typing programme; adapted PE participation; handwriting programme (Write from the Start, Speed Up)

classroom_strategies: Typing alternatives to handwriting
Tripod grip pen or pencil grip support
Extended time for written tasks
Adapted PE — focus on participation not performance
Seat with feet flat on floor, table at elbow height
Reduce copying from board — provide printed notes
parent_strategies: OT home programme implementation
Swimming and cycling as enjoyable motor development
Avoid pressure around motor tasks
Dyspraxia Ireland / Dyspraxia/DCD Ireland resources
research_links: EACD Recommendations for DCD (2019 update)
Missiuna et al. — CO-OP approach evidence
Dyspraxia Ireland — school guidance
Movement ABC-2 — Henderson, Sugden & Barnett (2007)

disorders.name: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
disorders.ep_note: Very common in high-achieving students and those with learning difficulties. EP role: psychoeducation in school, consultation to teachers, and contribution to intervention planning. Anxiety often secondary to unidentified SEN.
disorders.definition: Excessive, difficult-to-control anxiety and worry about multiple areas of life, present more days than not for at least 6 months, accompanied by physical symptoms, causing significant distress or functional impairment.
disorders.alert: Always ask what the child is anxious about — anxiety is often secondary to unidentified SEN (dyslexia, ADHD, ASD). Treat the underlying need, not just the anxiety. Excessive reassurance-seeking from teachers maintains anxiety — agree a brief consistent response.
criteria: Excessive anxiety and worry about multiple activities or events, present more days than not for ≥6 months
Difficulty controlling worry
3+ associated symptoms (1 in children): restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance
Causes significant distress or functional impairment
cognitive_mechanisms: Intolerance of uncertainty — worry as a coping strategy for uncertainty
Positive beliefs about worry ('worrying keeps bad things away')
Negative metacognition — worry about worrying
Catastrophisation and overestimation of threat
Hypervigilance to threat cues in environment
differential: Separation Anxiety (worry focused on separation specifically)
Social Anxiety (worry focused on social evaluation)

assessment_tools.name: RCMAS-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Revised Children's Manifest Anxiety Scale — total anxiety and subscales including physiological, worry, social concerns.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Standardised self-report for children 6–19. Good normative data. Widely used in EP reports.

assessment_tools.name: SCARED
assessment_tools.purpose: Screen for Child Anxiety Related Disorders — parent and child versions; maps to DSM anxiety disorder subtypes.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Free, downloadable, multi-informant. Useful triage and monitoring tool.

assessment_tools.name: MASC-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Multidimensional Anxiety Scale for Children — physical symptoms, harm avoidance, social anxiety, separation/panic.
assessment_tools.ep_note: More nuanced than RCMAS; useful when anxiety profile needs detailed mapping.

assessment_tools.name: SDQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Emotional symptoms scale as initial indicator.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Routinely used in NEPS/school consultations; emotional symptoms score >5 warrants follow-up.

Behaviour: Frequent reassurance-seeking from teachers ('Is this right?', 'What if I get it wrong?')
Perfectionism — erases repeatedly, cannot hand in work
Difficulty starting tasks — paralysed by uncertainty
Physical complaints (headaches, stomach aches) on school mornings or before tests
Academic & Social: Underperformance on assessments despite knowing material
Avoidance of challenging or uncertain tasks

home_signs: Worries about wide range of topics (world events, family safety, performance)
Difficulty falling asleep due to worrying
Seeks repeated reassurance from parents that escalates
Physical symptoms (nausea, stomach aches) before school
ep_formulation: Referral: somatic complaints, school avoidance, perfectionism, reassurance-seeking
Screen: SCARED parent and child; SDQ emotional symptoms
Rate anxiety: RCMAS-2 or MASC-2
Identify function: what does anxiety enable child to avoid?
Check for SEN: anxiety secondary to unidentified dyslexia/ADHD?
Formulate: GAD + contributing factors + functional impact in school
Recommend: CBT referral; school strategies; parent guidance on reassurance

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: CBT for anxiety (Coping Cat programme; FRIENDS programme) — cognitive restructuring, exposure hierarchy, relaxation

interventions.label: School / EP
interventions.text: Worry time strategy; predictable routines; brief consistent response to reassurance (not extended, not dismissive)

interventions.label: Family
interventions.text: Brief consistent response to reassurance-seeking; graduated exposure; modelling calm uncertainty tolerance

classroom_strategies: Predictable timetable — minimise unnecessary surprises
Clear instructions without ambiguity or open-ended options
Brief, consistent response to reassurance ('I know you can do this — give it a try')
Growth mindset around errors — model that mistakes are learning
Worry journal or box — designated worry time
parent_strategies: One brief, confident response to worry — then redirect
Tolerance for uncertainty modelling at home
Graduated exposure to feared situations — not avoidance
CAMHS/psychology referral if severe or persistent
research_links: NICE NG185 (2019) — Anxiety disorders in children and young people
Kendall — Coping Cat Programme (Workbook Child Anxiety Treatment)
FRIENDS for Life programme — Barrett et al.
Cathy Cresswell — Helping Your Child with Worries and Fears (Oxford Guides)

disorders.name: Emotionally Based School Non-Attendance (EBSNA)
disorders.ep_note: One of the most common and complex EP referral concerns in Ireland and UK. EP role is central: functional assessment of attendance, multi-agency coordination, reintegration planning, family and school consultation. Formerly called 'school refusal' — function-based approach is now recommended.
disorders.definition: A broad category describing persistent difficulty attending school that is rooted in emotional and psychological factors rather than truancy. Always requires functional assessment — the child's behaviour has a function (avoidance, escape, attention, or tangible rewards at home).
disorders.alert: EBSNA always has a function — identify it before intervening. Prolonged absence makes return harder. Firm, boundaried, early return is better than prolonged phased plans. Coordinate EP, CAMHS, EWO/Education Welfare Officer, and school urgently. In Ireland, TUSLA Education Support Service (TESS) involvement may be needed.
criteria: Difficulty attending school linked to emotional distress (not primarily truancy)
Significant anxiety, somatic complaints, or distress on school mornings
Parental awareness of and often accommodation of absence
Not primarily explained by truancy (which is purposeful, concealed from parents)
cognitive_mechanisms: Negative reinforcement — relief from avoided situation maintains avoidance
Positive reinforcement at home — screens, comfort, parental attention
Catastrophic appraisal of school situation
Anxiety about re-entering after absence (compounding over time)
differential: Truancy (purposeful, no parental knowledge — different intervention)
Unidentified SEN making school unbearable (SLD, ADHD, ASD)

assessment_tools.name: SRAS-R
assessment_tools.purpose: School Refusal Assessment Scale — Revised (Kearney). Identifies the function of school avoidance: avoidance of stimuli, escape from evaluation, parental attention, tangible rewards at home.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Essential first step — match intervention to function. Available for parent and child versions.

assessment_tools.name: SCARED
assessment_tools.purpose: Identify anxiety profile driving EBSNA.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Social anxiety, separation anxiety and GAD are most common drivers.

assessment_tools.name: MFQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Mood and Feelings Questionnaire — rule out depressive component.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Secondary depression from prolonged absence is common and must be addressed.

assessment_tools.name: Attendance data analysis
assessment_tools.purpose: Pattern of absence: which days, which lessons, which teachers, onset and triggers.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Start here — pattern often reveals function before any formal assessment.

Attendance: Persistent or gradually worsening absence — often starts after illness or holiday
Attendance linked to specific triggers (Monday, certain lessons, certain teachers)
Physical complaints dissolving once allowed to stay home
Texts or phone calls to parent during school day requesting collection
When Present: Distress at school gate at drop-off

home_signs: Distress Sunday evenings — dreading Monday
Somatic complaints (nausea, stomach aches) that improve once home
Physical symptoms absent at weekends and holidays
Parental anxiety about school also present
ep_formulation: Referral: worsening school absence with anxiety or somatic basis
Gather: attendance records; pattern analysis; parent interview
Functional assessment: SRAS-R (parent and child versions)
Assess: anxiety (SCARED); mood (MFQ); SEN profile
Identify: function + maintaining factors + school and home contributors
Develop: multi-agency plan — firm but graduated return; parallel CAMHS/therapy
Coordinate: EP, school, CAMHS, EWO, parents meeting urgently

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Function-matched CBT-based school attendance intervention — matched to Kearney SRAS-R function

interventions.label: Return Planning
interventions.text: Graduated but firm return to school — not indefinite phased plans. Shorter initial days with clear milestones

interventions.label: School / EP
interventions.text: Multi-agency meeting: school, EP, CAMHS, TUSLA/EWO, parents. Named key adult in school. Welcoming re-entry plan

interventions.label: Family
interventions.text: Brief confident school morning routine — reduce prolonged goodbyes. Reduce home reinforcement of absence. Psychoeducation on EBSNA maintenance

classroom_strategies: Warm, welcoming return — not punitive
Named key adult who checks in daily
Safe space pupil can use if overwhelmed
Flexible initial timetable with clear expansion schedule
Address specific fears directly (bully, teacher, subject)
Reduce demands initially — build back gradually
parent_strategies: Brief, confident school morning goodbye — no prolonged reassurance
Reduce home-based positive reinforcement of absence (screens, comfort activities)
School morning routine: up, breakfast, school — consistent and calm
Multi-agency coordination: attend meetings, support gradual return
TUSLA TESS support if needed (Ireland)
research_links: Kearney & Albano (2007) — When Children Refuse School: A Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Approach
NAHT — EBSNA: A Whole System Approach
TUSLA — Education Welfare Service guidance (Ireland)
EEF — Improving School Attendance toolkit

disorders.name: Selective Mutism
disorders.ep_note: EP role is critical in supporting understanding of SM in schools. Pressing children to speak worsens the condition. EP provides psychoeducation, functional communication hierarchy, and SALT consultation liaison.
disorders.definition: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (typically school) despite speaking comfortably in other situations (home, with close family). An anxiety disorder — not defiance, not shyness, not a language disorder.
disorders.alert: SM is an ANXIETY disorder — the child CAN speak but their anxiety prevents speaking. NEVER pressure direct speech — it worsens the condition. Teachers need EP psychoeducation urgently. Treat communication function before speaking.
criteria: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation to speak (school, social settings)
Speaks normally in other situations (home, with close family)
Interferes with educational achievement or social communication
Duration ≥1 month (not first month of school)
Not better explained by communication disorder or ASD
cognitive_mechanisms: Social anxiety as primary driver — speaking in front of others triggers freeze response
Avoidance of speaking reduces anxiety (negative reinforcement)
Behavioural inhibition temperament
Conditioned fear response to speaking in specific contexts
differential: Language Disorder (language difficulties across all contexts)
Bilingual/EAL adjustment (transient — not meeting SM criteria)

assessment_tools.name: SM Communication Hierarchy
assessment_tools.purpose: Map current and target communication contexts — from non-verbal to spoken communication in different settings.
assessment_tools.ep_note: EP constructs this collaboratively with school and family. Foundation of intervention planning.

assessment_tools.name: SCARED
assessment_tools.purpose: Social anxiety component — usually elevated in SM.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Provides anxiety profile; useful for CAMHS referral if needed.

Communication: No spoken communication in school or specific settings
Communicates through gesture, nod, whisper, writing, or technology
Speaks freely in some contexts (phone videos at home, to one close friend)
Facial expression may be 'frozen' in school
Behaviour: Appears anxious when verbal response expected
May be misread as rude, defiant or having language disorder

home_signs: Communicates freely and normally at home
Parents often shocked that school reports the child as silent
May be very chatty with close family
ep_formulation: Referral: child does not speak in school
Gather: speech and communication contexts (when, with whom, in what settings)
Distinguish: SM vs language disorder vs ASD vs elective mutism
Build communication hierarchy: non-verbal → functional communication → whisper → speech
SALT referral: SM-specialist SALT assessment and intervention
School psychoeducation: EP session with all staff — anxiety model, never force speech

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Sliding-In technique / Stimulus Fading — graduated introduction of new communication partners into safe communication contexts

interventions.label: Shaping
interventions.text: Shape communication from gesture → pointing → whispering → quiet speech → normal speech — reward any communication attempt

interventions.label: School
interventions.text: EP psychoeducation for all staff; agreed non-pressuring communication approach; AAC and technology as bridge

classroom_strategies: NEVER demand direct speech — anxiety worsens
Accept all forms of communication (gesture, nod, writing, technology)
Low-stakes communication opportunities (thumbs up/down, pointing)
Slide-in technique: familiar trusted adult brings new adult gradually into communication context
Reduce audience for any communication attempts
Ensure staff consistency — one rogue teacher who pressures can undo months of progress
parent_strategies: Do not avoid feared settings — graduated exposure
Praise any form of communication attempt
SMIRA resources and family guidance
Coordinate tightly with school and SALT
research_links: SMIRA — Selective Mutism Information and Research Association (UK)
Maggie Johnson — Selective Mutism: A Guide for Parents and Professionals
McHolm, Cunningham & Vanier — Helping Your Child with Selective Mutism

disorders.name: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
disorders.ep_note: EP role: trauma-informed educational assessment and school consultation. EPs do not treat PTSD but identify it, advocate for trauma-informed school environments, and coordinate with CAMHS/therapy services. Understanding trauma is essential for interpreting behaviour in schools.
disorders.definition: Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, followed by intrusion symptoms, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity, causing significant functional impairment.
disorders.alert: PTSD looks different in young children — play re-enactment, no sense of foreshortened future. In school, trauma behaviours (aggression, hypervigilance, dissociation, freezing) are frequently misread as ADHD, conduct disorder or defiance. TRAUMA INFORMS BEHAVIOUR — not bad character.
criteria: Exposure to actual or threatened trauma (direct, witnessed, learned it happened to close other)
Intrusion: recurrent memories, nightmares, flashbacks, psychological distress at reminders
Avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (thoughts, feelings, reminders)
Negative cognitions and mood: blame, negative beliefs about self/world, emotional numbing, alienation
Hyperarousal: hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance, irritability, reckless behaviour
Duration >1 month
cognitive_mechanisms: Disorganised trauma memory encoding — fragmented, contextualised by sensory cues
Dual representation theory — situationally accessible vs verbally accessible trauma memories
Chronic threat appraisal — world perceived as dangerous
Conditioned fear responses to trauma reminders (triggers)
Peritraumatic dissociation as risk factor for PTSD
differential: Complex PTSD (prolonged, multiple interpersonal trauma — affects identity and relationships)

assessment_tools.name: CPSS-5
assessment_tools.purpose: Child PTSD Symptom Scale — DSM-5 aligned self-report for children 8+.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful screening and monitoring tool in school context. Not diagnostic alone.

assessment_tools.name: CPSS-I
assessment_tools.purpose: Child PTSD Symptom Scale Interview — structured interview version.
assessment_tools.ep_note: More reliable than self-report for younger children or those with limited insight.

assessment_tools.name: Trauma History Checklist / ACEs screen
assessment_tools.purpose: Structured adverse childhood experiences assessment — quantify exposure and type.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Gather from parent and school records. EP should be aware of ACEs without detailed trauma interviewing of child.

Hyperarousal & Reactivity: Exaggerated startle response to sudden noises
Explosive anger or aggression appearing disproportionate to trigger
Cannot settle in class — sensory hyperarousal
Learning & Social: Significant academic decline following identified stressor
Avoidance of specific places, people or activities
Social withdrawal or re-enactment in play (younger children)

home_signs: Nightmares and sleep disturbance
Flashbacks or re-enactment in play
Regression in younger children
Irritability and anger at home
Clinging to caregivers
ep_formulation: Referral: behaviour change following identified event; known trauma history; concern raised
Do not conduct detailed trauma history with child — refer to CAMHS
Gather: teacher observations; parent report; school behaviour records
Screen: CPSS-5 with parental consent; ACEs awareness
Formulate: trauma-informed educational needs — not diagnostic
Recommend: trauma-informed whole-school approach; CAMHS TF-CBT referral; safe school environment

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Trauma-Focused CBT (TF-CBT) — gold standard for child trauma; includes parent component; delivered by CAMHS/clinical psychologist

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing) — NICE-approved for PTSD

interventions.label: School / EP
interventions.text: Trauma-informed whole-school approach: safety, predictability, trusted adult, flexible expectations, understanding behaviour as communication

classroom_strategies: Predictable, safe, calm environment — minimise unexpected changes
Named trusted adult with a clear, consistent role
Avoid known triggers where possible (specific sounds, spaces, topics)
Understand behaviour as trauma communication — not defiance
Flexible expectations during acute stress periods
Never restrain or isolate — can re-traumatise
parent_strategies: Maintain daily routines and predictability
Seek TF-CBT through CAMHS urgently
NSPCC and Barnardos trauma support resources (Ireland/UK)
research_links: NICE NG116 (2018) — PTSD: assessment and management
NSPCC — Trauma-informed practice resources
Porges — Polyvagal Theory (trauma-informed school lens)
Bruce Perry — The Boy Who Was Raised as a Dog

disorders.name: Looked After Children / Children in Care
disorders.ep_note: EP role is statutory and central in Ireland and UK. Every child in care should have an IEP (Ireland) or EHCP (UK). EP assessment supports care planning, placement stability and educational inclusion. In Ireland, EPs work with TUSLA and foster families. In UK, Virtual School Head coordinates with EP.
disorders.definition: Children in local authority care face substantially elevated rates of mental health difficulties (45–72%), neurodevelopmental conditions, attachment disorders, developmental trauma and educational disadvantage. Require coordinated multi-agency EP response.
disorders.alert: Up to 72% of looked after children have clinically significant mental health needs. Every LAC should have a Personal Education Plan (PEP). Developmental trauma affects ALL learning systems — cognition, language, emotion regulation and social development.
criteria: Child in care under Section 18 of Child Care Act 1991 (Ireland) or Children Act 1989 (UK)
Voluntary care or court order
Educational risk factors: trauma history, multiple placement moves, disrupted schooling
cognitive_mechanisms: Developmental trauma impacts all cognitive systems
Attachment disruption — negative internal working models affect learning relationships
Executive function and emotional regulation deficits
Language difficulties at higher prevalence
Hypervigilance reducing learning capacity
differential: Always assess for specific DSM diagnoses: PTSD, RAD, ADHD, SLD, ID

assessment_tools.name: SDQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire — statutory screening for LAC in both Ireland and UK.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Completed termly in UK. Provides baseline and tracking. Informs care planning.

assessment_tools.name: WISC-V / DAS-II
assessment_tools.purpose: Cognitive profile to inform IEP/EHCP targets and identify SEN.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Essential for LAC with educational concerns — often reveals unidentified SLD or ID.

assessment_tools.name: Vineland-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Adaptive functioning profile — often impaired relative to cognitive ability in LAC.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Informs realistic IEP targets based on real-world functioning rather than cognitive score.

Educational: History of multiple school moves — significant learning gaps
No EHC Plan/IEP despite high and complex needs
Relational: Attachment-seeking behaviour with teachers (clingy, or avoidant)
Hypervigilance — alert to adult mood and movement
Fight/flight/freeze responses that look like defiance or inattention
Difficulty forming trusting relationships with adults

home_signs: Placement instability (placement breakdown risk)
Carer capacity variation
Contact visit dysregulation — behaviour may deteriorate around contact
ep_formulation: EP assessment as part of PEP (Personal Education Plan) or EHCP
Cognitive and adaptive profile: WISC-V, Vineland-3
Identify: SEN (SLD, ADHD, ASD, ID, language disorder)
Trauma-informed formulation: behaviour in context of history
Collaborate: TUSLA/Social Worker, foster carer, Virtual School Head (UK)
Recommend: therapeutic educational provision; carer training; SEMH support

interventions.label: Education
interventions.text: Personal Education Plan (PEP) with realistic, trauma-informed targets; Pupil Premium Plus (UK); NCSE additional support

interventions.label: Therapeutic
interventions.text: Dyadic Developmental Psychotherapy (DDP — Hughes); TF-CBT; Circle of Security — after placement stability established

interventions.label: Foster Care
interventions.text: PACE parenting model (Playful, Accepting, Curious, Empathetic — Dan Hughes); therapeutic fostering training

classroom_strategies: Consistent, trusted named adult — key person relationship
PACE approach from all staff (Playful, Accepting, Curious, Empathetic)
Flexible behaviour management — understand the history
Celebrate attendance and effort, not just outcomes
Re-settle expectations after every placement move or disruption
parent_strategies: PACE parenting (Hughes) — training for foster carers
Multi-agency LAC review participation
Therapeutic fostering programme (Fostering Attachments)
TUSLA/social worker as central coordinator
research_links: NICE NG26 (2015) — Children's attachment
Dan Hughes — Building the Bonds of Attachment
TUSLA — Children in Care educational guidance (Ireland)
Virtual School Head statutory guidance (UK DfE)

disorders.name: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
disorders.ep_note: EP role: identification in school context, psychoeducation to staff, consultation on reasonable adjustments, CAMHS referral pathway. Depression in children presents as irritability as often as sadness. Always assess suicide risk if depression suspected.
disorders.definition: One or more major depressive episodes: at least 5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks including depressed mood or anhedonia, causing significant functional impairment.
disorders.alert: In children, depressed mood often presents as IRRITABILITY rather than sadness — easily missed. Never leave a suicide or self-harm concern without action. Always check with DSL/Designated Safeguarding Lead and follow safeguarding protocol. MFQ is free and validated — use it.
criteria: Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day (OR irritability in children and adolescents)
Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all activities
Significant weight change or appetite disturbance (or failure to gain weight in children)
Insomnia or hypersomnia
Psychomotor agitation or retardation
Fatigue or loss of energy
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt
Diminished concentration or indecisiveness
Recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation
cognitive_mechanisms: Beck's Cognitive Triad: negative view of self, world and future
Learned helplessness
Rumination — repetitive negative thinking maintaining depression
Anhedonia — disrupted reward processing and motivation
Hopelessness cognitions
differential: Dysthymia (Persistent Depressive Disorder — chronic, lower intensity)
Bipolar Disorder — screen for hypomanic episodes

assessment_tools.name: MFQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Mood and Feelings Questionnaire — child and parent versions. Free to use. Validated for 8–17 years.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Most widely used mood screen in UK/Ireland EP and CAMHS practice. Download free from MRC Cambridge.

assessment_tools.name: RCADS
assessment_tools.purpose: Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale — covers both anxiety and depression with normative data.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Good for dual anxiety-depression presentations. Free online. Used in IAPT/CAMHS.

assessment_tools.name: PHQ-A
assessment_tools.purpose: Patient Health Questionnaire — Adolescent version. Brief 9-item depression screen.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Widely used in GP and CAMHS settings; useful for secondary school-age pupils.

Academic: Difficulty concentrating — appears distracted or absent
Incomplete work, stops handing in assignments
Withdraws from previously enjoyed school activities
Social & Emotional: Isolation at breaks and lunch — sits alone
Irritability and low frustration tolerance (especially younger children)

home_signs: Persistent sadness or tearfulness
Loss of interest in hobbies, sport, social activities
Sleep disturbance (too much or too little)
Appetite changes
Withdrawal from family
Statements about hopelessness, worthlessness or death
ep_formulation: Concern raised: unexplained academic decline, withdrawal, teacher or parent concern
Screen: MFQ parent and child; check for suicidal ideation
If suicidal ideation: immediate DSL involvement + CAMHS urgent referral
Assess: RCADS (anxiety-depression profile); school functioning
Liaise: CAMHS referral; pastoral team; school counsellor
Recommend: CAMHS psychological assessment; reasonable adjustments in school; monitoring

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: CBT for Depression — individual and group (NICE first-line for mild-moderate)

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: Interpersonal Therapy for Adolescents (IPT-A) — particularly for relationship-linked depression

interventions.label: Medical
interventions.text: CAMHS assessment — Fluoxetine (SSRI) if CBT insufficient; under CAMHS psychiatric supervision

interventions.label: School / EP
interventions.text: Reasonable adjustments: reduced timetable, alternative formats, pastoral monitoring, safe space access

classroom_strategies: Warm, positive relationship with teacher — most protective factor
Celebrate contributions and effort — not just attainment
Involve in meaningful roles and responsibilities
Avoid public critique or humiliation
Reduced workload during acute episode
Safe space access when overwhelmed
parent_strategies: Open, non-judgemental conversations about feelings
Limit social media during acute episode
Promote physical activity — modest but evidenced
CAMHS referral — do not wait and see if persistent
research_links: NICE CG28 (2019 update) — Depression in children and young people
MFQ — free download from MRC Cambridge Unit
MindEd — School staff mental health resources
Young Minds — Parent and school resources (UK)
Jigsaw — Ireland's national youth mental health programme

disorders.name: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)
disorders.ep_note: ODD is often a secondary presentation of unmet needs — ADHD, anxiety, ASD, learning difficulties or trauma. EP role: functional behavioural assessment, identifying underlying drivers, consultation to school on PBS approach.
disorders.definition: A persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour and vindictiveness toward adults or authority figures, causing significant distress or functional impairment in ≥1 context.
disorders.alert: ODD is almost always secondary to something else. ALWAYS assess for underlying ADHD, anxiety, ASD, SLD, trauma or adverse experiences before treating ODD as a primary condition. Treating the underlying need dramatically reduces oppositional behaviour.
criteria: 4+ symptoms for ≥6 months from: loses temper, touchy/easily annoyed, angry and resentful, argues with adults, actively defies rules, deliberately annoys others, blames others, spiteful or vindictive (≥2× in 6 months)
Disturbance causes distress or impacts social, educational or occupational functioning
cognitive_mechanisms: Hostile attribution bias — interprets neutral situations as threatening or intentionally provocative
Emotional dysregulation — rapid escalation
Maladaptive appraisal of authority
ADHD executive function making compliance harder
Anxiety-driven control behaviour in some children
differential: ADHD (co-occurring ~50% — non-compliance from EF not defiance)

assessment_tools.name: SDQ
assessment_tools.purpose: Conduct problems scale; externalising profile.
assessment_tools.ep_note: First-line screen in school context. Provides teacher and parent comparison.

assessment_tools.name: CBCL
assessment_tools.purpose: Child Behaviour Checklist (Achenbach) — externalising and internalising profile.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Comprehensive multi-informant tool. Useful when clinical picture is complex.

assessment_tools.name: Conners-3
assessment_tools.purpose: Assess co-occurring ADHD and ODD.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Identifies whether opposition is ADHD-driven or primary ODD — changes intervention.

Behaviour: Blames others consistently for own mistakes
Refuses reasonable requests as a pattern
Escalates rapidly when challenged or corrected

home_signs: Persistent arguments about household rules and limits
Blames siblings and parents for everything
Refuses reasonable parental requests
ep_formulation: Referral: non-compliance, defiance, disruptive behaviour
Assess: Conners-3 (rule out ADHD); SDQ; trauma history
Functional behaviour assessment: what triggers defiance? What does it achieve?
Check: ASD (rigidity), anxiety (control), SLD (avoidance of difficulty)
Recommend: PBS; parent management training; CPS approach; treat ADHD if present

interventions.text: Positive Behaviour Support — function-based, proactive approach; STAR charts not punishments

interventions.label: Medical

classroom_strategies: Relationship first — positive attention ratio (5:1 positive to corrective)
Avoid power struggles — offer two positive choices
Private corrective feedback — never public humiliation
Predictable, fair expectations communicated calmly
Collaborative problem solving approach to conflicts
parent_strategies: Parent Management Training programme with CAMHS or psychology
Reduce attention to minor misbehaviour — planned ignoring
Ross Greene — The Explosive Child (practical framework)
Treat ADHD if co-occurring — usually transforms ODD presentations

disorders.name: ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder)
disorders.ep_note: Strongly associated with ASD, ADHD and anxiety. EP role: advise school on mealtime management, sensory considerations, and coordinate with OT and SLT. School lunch is a major distress point for ARFID children.
disorders.definition: Restriction of food intake by amount or type — not driven by body image concerns — resulting in significant nutritional/weight impact, supplement dependence, or psychosocial impairment.
disorders.alert: ARFID is NOT Anorexia Nervosa — there is NO body image disturbance. The restriction is driven by sensory sensitivity, fear, or low interest in food — not by desire to lose weight. Never force eating. School mealtimes can be severely distressing.
criteria: Restriction in amount or type of food: significant weight loss or failure to gain, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements, significant psychosocial impairment
Not better explained by food unavailability or cultural practices
Not occurring exclusively during AN or BN
Not attributable to medical/GI condition or another mental disorder
cognitive_mechanisms: Sensory sensitivity — texture, smell, colour, temperature of food
Conditioned aversive response (choking, gagging, vomiting fear)
Low interest in food as primary feature in some
Anxiety-based avoidance of unfamiliar foods
differential: ASD-related food selectivity (high overlap — may co-occur)
risk_factors: History of choking or vomiting trauma

assessment_tools.name: PARDI
assessment_tools.purpose: Pica, ARFID and Rumination Disorder Interview — gold standard structured diagnostic interview.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Requires specialist training. EP may review findings in MDT context.

assessment_tools.name: 9-Item ARFID Screen (NIAS)
assessment_tools.purpose: Brief validated screening questionnaire for ARFID.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Useful for initial screening in school context to support referral.

assessment_tools.name: Sensory Profile-2
assessment_tools.purpose: Assess sensory processing differences including oral sensory sensitivity.
assessment_tools.ep_note: Helps identify sensory contribution to food restriction — informs OT referral.

Eating: Extremely limited food repertoire — brings same 'safe' foods daily
Unable to eat school dinners — significant distress at lunch
Gags or vomits in response to non-preferred foods
Anxiety before and during meal times
Social: Cannot attend school trips or social events involving food
Birthday celebrations and food-sharing events are distressing

home_signs: Eats only 5–15 'safe' foods — strong family stress around mealtimes
Family cannot eat together due to food restrictions
Parental concern about nutritional adequacy
ep_formulation: Referral: extreme food selectivity, distress at school mealtimes, weight concerns
Sensory profile: assess oral sensory sensitivity
ASD/anxiety screen: very high comorbidity
Nutritional concern: refer to paediatrician/dietitian if weight or nutrition impacted
Recommend: safe food provision at school; OT sensory desensitisation referral; CBT-AR if appropriate

interventions.label: Evidence-Based
interventions.text: CBT-AR (Cognitive Behavioural Treatment for ARFID — Thomas & Eddy 2019) — exposure-based approach

interventions.label: School
interventions.text: Individual mealtime plan: safe food option available; no pressure; alternative seating; quiet exit option

classroom_strategies: Ensure safe food is always available at lunch (cater from home if needed)
Do not force food exposure or tasting in school
Reduce social pressure at mealtimes — offer quiet eating option
OT referral for sensory desensitisation programme
Never use food as reward or punishment
parent_strategies: Graduated exposure hierarchy with ARFID-trained therapist — not at home alone
Do not pressure, bribe or punish around food
Dietitian monitoring of nutritional intake
ARFID Awareness UK resources
research_links: Thomas & Eddy (2019) — CBT-AR treatment manual
ARFID Awareness UK
